stories.title: Man charged following public order incident in Louth
stories.summary: A man has been charged in relation to a public order incident in Co Louth where gardaí used "less-lethal force" to disarm a person. The incident took place at around 9.30pm at a car park in Dundalk and involved uniformed gardaí working alongside members of the Armed Support Unit. In a statement, gardaí said they had engaged with a man armed with a knife to try and de-escalate the situation. The man did not comply and that "gardaí from the Armed Support Unit discharged one round from a 40mm less-lethal force option".

stories.title: Chris Bryant appointed as new Northern Ireland Secretary
stories.summary: Chris Bryant has been appointed to serve as the new Secretary of State for Northern Ireland. The former minister for trade and labour was announced by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a long-running process to appoint his Cabinet. The announcement came just after 11pm last night after it emerged earlier that Hilary Benn would not be continuing in the role. Mr Bryant, a former Anglican priest, has been the MP for Rhondda and Ogmore, and previously Rhondda, in Wales, since 2001.

stories.title: Iran targets US military sites, Houthis make port threats
stories.summary: Iran has targeted US radar and air defence installations in the Gulf, warning the US of "more decisive and powerful" attacks to come as the conflict threatened to widen with a blockade of Saudi ports by Houthi rebels in Yemen. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked and stopped two "non-compliant oil tankers" attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, part of an effort to tighten its grip on the vital waterway while the war reignited. Following the deaths of at least three US soldiers in the past several days, the United States launched a new round of attacks against Iran which it said were "designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping" in the strait. Hours later, the Iranian army said it had targeted US assets in Kuwait and Bahrain, including air defence systems, radar installations and administrative buildings.

stories.title: How can a country as wet as Ireland need hosepipe bans?
stories.summary: Ireland is one of Europe's wettest countries. Depending on where you live, rain falls on between 199 and 273 days a year. So why, after just a few weeks of warm weather, are hundreds of thousands of people being told not to use their hosepipe? Ireland receives plenty of rain, but only a fraction of it will ever reach a household tap. Some rain evaporates, some is absorbed into soil, some flows back to the sea, and only part of what remains is captured, treated and delivered through the public water network. "Ireland doesn't have a rainfall problem," says Dr Shaun Harrigan, Assistant Professor of Hydroclimatology at Maynooth University. "We sometimes have a water storage and treated supply problem."

stories.title: McGrath in favour of age-appropriate social media limits
stories.summary: EU Commissioner Michael McGrath has said that he agrees with age-appropriate social media restrictions for children and teenagers rather than an outright ban. It follows a report from an expert panel on child safety that under-13s should only be allowed to use social media for limited periods under the supervision of parents, caregivers and teachers. The restrictions would then be lifted ⁠gradually as teenagers got older. "There would be additional more onerous obligations on social media companies to ensure that their service is safe for children of that age and so it's a graduated age-related approach is what they have recommended, rather than an outright ban up to the age of 16," Mr McGrath said.

stories.title: Trump orders new 50% tariff on many Canadian goods
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has signed orders to impose new 50% tariffs on many Canadian goods, claiming "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against American alcohol, automobile and dairy products. The tariffs take effect in 30 days and cover various items including wine, hockey sticks and cement, said the White House. Mr Trump, who saw many of his tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court this year, tapped an untested legal provision for the new duties - Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The latest duties will not apply to energy, potash and goods already impacted by sector-specific tariffs.
